Why these gauges describe stress but cannot forecast it: see the guide.

Behavioral guardrail — brake yourself, not the market strong evidence · about you

Aimed at the one lever the evidence says matters most for outcomes — your behaviour, not the market (the evidence is about investor behaviour in general; this journal itself is untested). It audits your decisions, holds your pre-commitments, and adds a pause exactly where panic happens. Walled off from every market reading by design.

Volatility-sizing dial — a down-only throttle risk, not alpha

Size down when forecast volatility exceeds the comfort band you type — it caps at 100% (never levers up); you set the band and pull the lever. Shown with the honest drawdown↔turnover trade-off, no Sharpe.

Crash-context badge — the regime you're already in coincident, not a forecast

A pure annotation: turbulence, absorption (variance share of the top modes, vs its own history), shock clustering and skew read together as the current tail regime. Wired to nothing — it moves no dial and predicts nothing.

Diversification reality check fair-weather caveat

How many bets you really have and how few names carry your risk — with the honest warning that average correlations understate how they collapse in a crisis.

Contrarian sentiment thermometer context only

Panic / neutral / euphoria from VIX, valuation and turbulence extremes — shown with the forward-return distribution from here as proof it's a thermometer, not a clock. No trade, no buy/sell, ever.

Stress test — simulated bad months for a size you already chose simulated from real moves · not a forecast

Builds 2,000 possible next months by replaying SPY's real daily moves, resized to today's volatility. Use it to test whether you could live with your position size in a bad month.

Drift & rebalance — a state, not an alert band, not a trigger

Where a year of relative performance has pushed your mix off the target weights you set in the Crisis-replay card — shown as a passive state. Never a red action; rebalance on a rule, not a signal.

Stock-bond ballast read describes the past quarter

Whether bonds are currently diversifying your equities or moving with them (like 2022) — present-tense context for your ballast, with no persistence claim and no allocation steer.

Directed spillover network — who leads whom

An arrow from A to B means A's past moves line up with B's later moves more than the other way round. Solid arrows pass a chance check; dashed ones do not. Red markets mostly lead, blue mostly follow. Lining up is not causing. Closing times: exchange rates are ECB reference rates set at about 8:15am ET, and crypto days close at 00:00 UTC (7pm ET in winter, 8pm in summer), so a one-day lead between either of them and a US market is partly a timing effect.
net transmitter (leads) net receiver (lags)

Asymmetry matrix & net transmitter / receiver

Left: each square compares a pair both ways: red means the row market leads the column market, blue the reverse, white neither. Right: each market's net lead (right, red) or follow (left, blue). Leads between US markets and exchange rates or crypto are partly closing-time effects (see the spillover network card).

Cascade what-if — how far a shock could spread what-if, not a forecast

Pick a market and see which others a shock there could reach through the lead-lag links, at the link strength you set. A what-if on today's estimated links, not a forecast. Links between US markets and exchange rates or crypto are partly closing-time effects (see the spillover network card).

Network structure — hubs, choke points & amplification network shape

Where the links bunch up (hubs), which market's removal would most cut how far a shock spreads (choke point), and whether the network spreads or damps a shock. Links between US markets and exchange rates or crypto are partly closing-time effects (see the spillover network card).

Systemic coupling — how much the basket moves as one

How much the whole basket moves as one. Coupling runs from near 0 (independent) to 1 (all together). Absorption is the share of all movement in the ten biggest shared patterns. High readings leave less room to absorb a shock.

Factor baskets — what actually moves together hierarchical · empirical

Many of these 48 markets move together. This groups them by how they actually move; markets in one basket are not separate bets.

Crowd behaviour — why prices are hard to call framing

Why prices are hard to call (everyone is guessing what everyone else will do), and when conditions favour a rush for the exit: moves reinforcing each other, many markets stretched, the most connected market changing.

Resting buy vs sell orders — live crypto order book crypto · seconds · descriptive

How much is waiting to buy versus sell in the Binance.US order book now, refreshed every few seconds. Waiting orders, not where price will go.

Turbulence — how unusual today's combined move is

Compares today's moves across all markets with the past year's usual pattern, as a 0 to 100 rank against that year.
0.20

Market map — which past stretches looked like today

Each dot is a 10-day stretch of market moves; similar stretches sit close together. Resemblance does not mean the same outcome follows.

Anticipation — the most connected market & a held-out lead test predictive test

Names the market whose volatility moves with the most others, and tests on later, unseen years whether its stress shows up before the rest. It cannot tell which market moves first.
Strategy test (Alpha Lab) — does trading on stress pay after costs? research · net-of-cost
Tests a simple rule that trades when stress is high, on years it was not tuned on, after costs, against just holding SPY. Verdict: works, does not work, or not enough evidence.
Crisis replay — your mix through past stress windows historical · not predictive
Set the weights you choose and replay them, daily-rebalanced, through a real past stress window. Pure historical replay of data already in the console — no model, no forecast, no recommendation. It shows how a mix actually held up, and how its protection shrank as assets coupled.
Income mix — real yields and real drawdowns education · not advice
Split a sum across six kinds of holding and see the income today's published yields would pay, next to the worst falls the same mix took in real past markets. Each yield shows its source and date; international has no yield in the page and is left out of the income.

Volatility forecast — predict what can be predicted tested on unseen data

Tests how well today's readings predict how bumpy the next 5 and 20 days will be, and which way prices go, on data the model did not see. R² of 0 or less means no skill.

Forecast reliability — when to trust the volatility forecast calm, middle, stormy

Predicts nothing itself: it shows how well the volatility forecast has done on calm, middle and stormy days (each a third of days, sorted by the past 20 days' volatility), so you know when to trust it.

Overnight vs daytime returns risk premium · show, not trade

Splits each day into overnight (close to next open) and daytime (open to close). Most of the long-run gain came overnight: pay for holding overnight risk, not a trading edge.

Long-horizon valuation thermometer years · descriptive

How expensive US stocks are against their own history (Shiller's price-to-earnings ratio, 1881 on). High prices have meant lower returns over the next ten years on average, with very wide error; nothing about the next months.

Factor companion — trend, carry, low risk cross-asset · descriptive

Three patterns that have paid over 1 to 12 months across many markets. Shown as today's posture, not a signal to trade.

Forward macro — recession & financial conditions months horizon

Where the best free forward-content data actually carries signal: the yield curve, credit spreads, and financial-conditions index — leading recession and stress at a months horizon (not days). The constructive complement to the vol lab's finding that these overfit a short-horizon model.

Backtest replay — what the gauges said on past dates

Walk-forward where it matters: at the cursor date the network, coupling, turbulence, Hawkes, thermometer and briefing use only data up to that day (the operator wiki lists the panels that don't). This table does not move with the cursor: it scores fragility over the selected asset's whole history against what actually happened next — and compares it to the unconditional base rate, because with only a handful of real drawdown events, apparent "skill" is mostly luck.

In plain English — what the latest data says

Auto-written from the latest readings (live feeds if reachable, otherwise the embedded snapshot — the heading says which date), for a non-specialist. Updates with the data (and with the cursor in Backtest).

Perspectives — ten investing stances interpretive, not predictive

Today's readings seen from ten common investing stances. Written by this console from the data; not anyone's words, views or advice.

Structural backdrop — distribution & real economy

Slow-moving US data on wealth, income, saving, housing and rates, for background. Published quarterly or yearly; not a trading signal.
value = latest / as-of cursorright column = ~10-year change (pp for rates & shares, % otherwise)

Fragility thermometer sort: basket ▾

0–100 = how unusually fast each asset's fragility indicators have been rising (their 60-day trend) versus its own history, on three channels (persistence · amplitude · tail). A rate of change, not a level: a steadily volatile asset reads ~50. High ≠ crash; it can persist for years. Three mini-bars = the sub-scores.
calmelevatedleast resilient vs own norm mini-bars: persist amplitude tail

Indicator detail —

The seven measures behind this market's score, in three groups: how long moves persist, how big they are, how lopsided the tails are. They overlap; they are not seven separate votes.

Surprise — how unexpected today's move was

How surprising today's move is to a simple model of each market's recent behaviour (0 to 100, higher = more surprising).

Shock clustering — do big moves come in bunches?

Counts days with unusually large moves and asks whether they bunch together more than chance: 0 = no bunching, near 1 = each shock sets off another. It counts only if it beats the same shocks shuffled in time.

Data health

Embedded real-history snapshot is the floor; live endpoints refresh the tail when reachable. A single feed failure never blanks the console. Cross-asset panels only use dates every market in the panel shares: all 51 for the directed network (so in Backtest it is empty before crypto starts on 2023-09-21), and the 48 non-crypto names for coupling, turbulence and the manifold (back to 2016). A series that stops early holds back every panel that includes it, so the as-of date is the oldest series end shown below. Macro (FRED) is published on a daily schedule and checked anonymously from this site; original observation dates and the embedded fallback stay visible. CAPE (Shiller) remains a separately dated embedded snapshot.

Macro update status

Embedded macro fallback; observation periods are shown separately from source retrieval.
